title: Already happened
goal: Tell about completed events with the perfect, find the perfect stem in the third dictionary form, and choose between the imperfect and the perfect.
bekal: form all six perfect forms from any stem
memorize the five most common perfect-stem patterns
decide for yourself when to use *ambulabam* and when *ambulavi*

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Elephantus in foro
dialogs.intro: Marcus comes home from the forum with news that's hard to believe.

notes: **The perfect endings are unlike any other tense.** *-i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt*. Note that the "I" form ends in *-i* and the "they" form in *-erunt* — two endings that appear in no other tense. As soon as you see them, you know the sentence is about something already finished.

**Vidi, dixi, duxi, veni — the stem must be memorized.** The perfect is not built on the ordinary stem but on a stem of its own, listed in the dictionary as the third part: *video, videre, **vidi***; *dico, dicere, **dixi***; *venio, venire, **veni***. This is the only part of the Latin verb system that really has to be learned word by word.

**Stabam et spectabam, deinde spectavit.** Look at the switch in line eight. The first two verbs use the imperfect because they paint an ongoing state; the third uses the perfect because one sudden event cuts in. This is how every Latin author tells a story: the scene in the imperfect, the surprise in the perfect.

**Cecidit and cucurri — stems that repeat a syllable.** A group of old verbs forms its perfect stem by repeating the first syllable: *cado* → *cecidi*, *curro* → *cucurri*, *do* → *dedi*, *cano* → *cecini*, *disco* → *didici*. These doubled forms are left over from a layer of the language much older than Rome itself.

sections.title: The perfect: one set of endings for every group

blocks.text: Unlike the other tenses, the perfect doesn't care which group a verb belongs to. Take the perfect stem, add the same six endings, done.
You get the perfect stem by dropping the *-i* from the third dictionary form: *portavi* → *portav-*, *vidi* → *vid-*, *dixi* → *dix-*. No insert, no linking letter, no difference between groups.

blocks.title: Two traps to watch for
items: *venit* can mean "he comes" (present) **or** "he came". The Romans told them apart by vowel length, which isn't written. Context helps you: if you see *heri*, *deinde*, or *subito*, it's almost certainly the perfect.
*legit*, *fugit*, *vertit* have the same kind of twin. The list is short, and all are group-three verbs whose perfect stem matches the ordinary stem.
*Vidimus* is always "we saw", never "we see" — because the present is *videmus*, with an *e*. That one-letter difference matters.

blocks.text: Perfect stems do have to be memorized, but they aren't completely random. Almost all of them fall into one of the five patterns below, and recognizing the pattern makes memorizing much lighter.

head: Pattern
Sign
Example
Mainly in group
rows: porto → portavi; amo → amavi; audio → audivi
habeo → habui; doceo → docui; timeo → timui
dico → dixi; duco → duxi; scribo → scripsi; mitto → misi
video → vidi; venio → veni; lego → legi; facio → **feci** (a becomes e)
cado → cecidi; curro → cucurri; do → dedi; disco → didici

blocks.text: Notice three you have known all your life: *vici* from Caesar's *veni, vidi, vici*; *fui*, which appears on Roman tombstones; and *dixi*, still used to close a speech — "I have spoken".
English often lets you blur the two with a simple past; Latin makes you choose. Luckily, the choice comes down to one question: does the action have an end point?

head: Imperfect
Perfect
The difference
rows: "I used to live in Rome" — versus — "I lived in Rome (and that's over)"
"he was telling a story" — versus — "he told a story"
a description of the scene — versus — a finished statement

blocks.title: Close cousins not taught yet
items: **Had done** (*pluperfect*): perfect stem + *-eram*. *Veneram* — "I had come (before something else happened)". Easy to guess once you know the perfect stem.
**Will have done** (*future perfect*): perfect stem + *-ero*. *Venero* — "I will have come". Common in clauses with *si* and *cum*.
Neither is practiced in this book, but you already have all the pieces. If you meet them in a text, identify the stem first, then the ending.
